title: Shell Text Pipelines: Pipes, grep, sed, awk and Friends
summary: Quick revision notes on chaining Unix text tools with pipes and redirection, covering grep, sed, awk, cut, sort, uniq, wc, head, tail, xargs and basic regular expressions. It ends with the common mistakes and a one-page cheat sheet.

chapters.title: Streams, Pipes and Redirection Model
points: Every process has three streams: stdin (fd 0), stdout (fd 1), stderr (fd 2); a filter reads stdin and writes stdout
Pipe `a | b` connects a's stdout to b's stdin; both run at the same time and only stdout travels, not stderr
`>` truncates and writes a file, `>>` appends, `<` feeds a file to stdin
`2>file` redirects stderr, `2>&1` merges stderr into stdout, `&>file` captures both (bash); order matters: `cmd >f 2>&1` works, `cmd 2>&1 >f` does not
Gotcha: `sort f > f` empties f before sort reads it; write to a temp file or use `sort -o f f`

chapters.title: Searching with grep and Regex Basics
points: `grep PATTERN file` prints matching lines; key flags: -i ignore case, -v invert, -n line numbers, -c count, -r recursive, -l filenames only
Regex anchors and wildcards: `^` start of line, `$` end of line, `.` any one character, `*` zero or more of the previous item
Character classes: `[abc]` one of, `[^abc]` none of, `[0-9]`, and `\d`-style shortcuts only in -P; POSIX classes like `[[:digit:]]`
BRE vs ERE: plain grep needs `\+ \? \| \( \)`, while `grep -E` (egrep) uses `+ ? | ( )` unescaped; use -E by default
Gotchas: quote the pattern so the shell does not expand `*`; use -F for literal text such as `grep -F 'a.b'`; `grep -w` matches whole words, `-o` prints only the match

chapters.title: Slicing and Counting: cut, sort, uniq, wc, head, tail
points: `cut -d, -f1,3` picks delimited fields and `cut -c1-5` picks characters; the default delimiter is TAB
`sort` flags: -n numeric, -r reverse, -k2 by field 2, -t, set delimiter, -u unique; the default order is lexical, so 10 comes before 2
`uniq` collapses only adjacent duplicates, so run `sort | uniq`; `uniq -c` counts and `-d` shows only duplicates
`wc -l` lines, `-w` words, `-c` bytes; `head -n 5` and `tail -n 5` show the first or last lines, `tail -n +2` skips the header, `tail -f` follows a growing file
Top-N idiom: `cut -d' ' -f1 access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr | head`

chapters.title: Transforming Text with sed and awk
points: `sed 's/old/new/g'` substitutes on every line; without g only the first match per line changes; the delimiter can be any character, e.g. `s|/usr|/opt|`
sed options: -n with `p` prints only matching lines (`sed -n '5,10p'`), `/re/d` deletes lines, -i edits the file in place (GNU: `-i.bak` keeps a backup)
awk model: `pattern { action }` runs per line; fields are $1..$NF, $0 is the whole line, NR is the line number, -F, sets the field separator
awk examples: `awk '$3 > 100 {print $1}'` filters then prints, and `awk '{s+=$2} END{print s}'` sums a column using the END block
Choosing: cut for simple column pulls, sed for line edits and substitution, awk for per-field logic, conditions and arithmetic

chapters.title: Building Pipelines with xargs and Avoiding Mistakes
points: `xargs` turns whitespace-separated stdin items into arguments for a command: `grep -l TODO *.c | xargs wc -l`; it is needed because many commands ignore stdin
Filenames with spaces break xargs; use `find . -name '*.log' -print0 | xargs -0 rm` for safe NUL-separated input
`xargs -n1` runs one argument per call, `-I{}` places the argument anywhere (`xargs -I{} cp {} /backup`), `-P4` runs 4 jobs in parallel
Pipeline exit status is that of the last command only; `set -o pipefail` makes a failing stage fail the whole pipeline
Mistakes: useless `cat file | grep` (use `grep x file`), `uniq` without `sort`, unquoted patterns, and running `rm` through xargs before previewing with `echo`

chapters.title: Pipelines Cheat Sheet
points: Redirection: `> >> < 2> 2>&1 | tee file` (tee writes to a file and passes the data on)
Columns and order: `cut -d, -f2`, `sort -t, -k2 -nr`, `sort | uniq -c`, `wc -l`, `head -n`, `tail -n +2`
sed and awk one-liners: `sed 's/a/b/g'`, `sed -n '3,5p'`, `sed '/x/d'`, `awk -F, '{print $1}'`, `awk '$2>10'`, `awk '{s+=$1} END{print s}'`
Recipes: top-N `sort | uniq -c | sort -nr | head`, safe delete `find -print0 | xargs -0 echo rm`, count matches `grep -c`
